notable_anecdotes: Quantitative dimension: Carandang ponencia 235 pages with 560 footnotes; Gesmundo separate opinion 199 pages with 762 footnotes (202 more); 11 justices wrote separate opinions totaling 640 pages -- making the column the second installment of a two-part deep dive.

Gesmundo's voted-and-prevailed instances: outvoted in many places, but won 9-6 on Section 10's last paragraph and 8-7 on the Section 25 'third mode of designation' -- CJ specifically highlights these two near-misses.

The 'organized for the purpose of engaging in terrorism' phrase in Section 10 was the ponente's vagueness target; CJ argues with Gesmundo that Section 4's clear acts make the phrase non-vague (one of the few places CJ takes a directly anti-libertarian position).

Gesmundo's bolded language: 'In dealing with terrorism, we should utilize all possible kinds of legally available measures and approaches--pre-emptive, preventive, proactive, remedial, and rehabilitative...' -- a five-mode terrorism-response framework reproduced verbatim.
Vote-of-7 'DISMISS OUTRIGHT' on 33 of 37 petitions 'for failure to satisfy the requirements of judicial review' -- and then dismissal even of the four admitted ones 'for lack of merit.'

Closing advice to civil-liberties petitioners: shift from facial challenges to 'low-intensity, libertarian as-applied challenges' as the ATA is enforced -- a strategic concession that frontal constitutional attack has failed but operational litigation remains viable.

one_paragraph_summary: In the second installment of his two-part deep dive into Calleja v. Executive Secretary (Dec. 7, 2021, released Feb. 15, 2022), Panganiban turns from Justice Carandang's 235-page ponencia (with 560 footnotes) to Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo's 'masterfully-crafted and delightful to read' 199-page separate opinion (with 762 footnotes, 202 more than the ponencia), which firmly upholds the Anti-Terrorism Act's constitutionality in contrast to the ponencia's libertarian leanings. Gesmundo, advocating that 'we should utilize all possible kinds of legally available measures and approaches -- pre-emptive, preventive, proactive, remedial, and rehabilitative' against terrorism without 'overzealous legalism, imaginative speculation, or very narrow perspectives,' joined six other justices in voting to admit only four of 37 petitions and 'DISMISS OUTRIGHT' the remaining 33, then dismissed the four admitted petitions 'for lack of merit' using strict scrutiny without overbreadth/vagueness. With Justice Marquez, he argued that the ATA penalizes only overt acts including 'speech integral to criminal conduct,' and that as-applied challenges don't foreclose the use of vagueness/overbreadth as tools of scrutiny. Though outvoted in many places, Gesmundo prevailed in two: a 9-6 vote upholding Section 10's last paragraph on membership in proscribed or 'organized for the purpose of engaging in terrorism' organizations (where CJ Panganiban agrees with him against the ponente's vagueness finding), and an 8-7 vote upholding Section 25's 'third mode of designation' empowering the ATC to designate on probable cause and the AMLC to freeze accounts. AT BOTTOM, with only Section 4's PROVISO and Section 25 paragraph 2's 'second mode of designation' struck, 'the government, IMHO, emerged the clear winner' -- 'a little scathed' but intact -- and the petitioners' 71-page Joint Motion for Reconsideration 'pales in comparison' with the exhaustive opinions; their best path forward, with due respect, is to 'wage low-intensity, libertarian as-applied challenges' as the ATA is enforced.
